introduction.text: **Before you start.** Preserving turns a glut into a pantry: late-summer cucumbers into pickles, autumn cabbage into sauerkraut, plums into jam, duck legs into confit. It is also where a home cook's mistake can be most dangerous, because the worst hazard, botulism, cannot be seen, smelled or tasted. So this course works by one rule: **every method is a tested method**, from a named source, followed exactly where safety depends on it. The course has six parts:

items.text: **principles:** the hurdles behind each method, and how to spot an unsafe recipe;
**pickling:** quick fridge pickles by ratio, and water-bath canning of an acid pickle by a tested recipe;
**lacto-fermentation:** sauerkraut at a weighed salt percentage, a mixed ferment, and telling normal from spoiled;
**salt curing and confit:** a cure by weight, and confit stored safely;
**drying and sugar preserves:** a low oven, a jam and a chutney;
**cooking with preserves:** the pantry used, labelled and rotated.
the pH line of 4.6 between acid and low-acid foods;
home canning of acid foods only, in boiling water, by a tested recipe;
sauerkraut salt at 2.25–2.5 % with its temperatures and times;
nitrite curing salt only where a tested recipe needs it, at most 80 mg of nitrite per kg of meat;
garlic and herbs in oil kept in the fridge;
the fridge at 4 °C, leftovers kept at most 2 days, the cooling standard.

introduction.text: The tested recipes come from the National Center for Home Food Preservation (NCHFP) [S27], named in each lesson. The Netherlands lies at sea level, so a tested recipe's lowest-altitude processing time is the one to use.

The produce follows the Dutch harvest: cucumbers, beans, courgettes and beetroot in late summer; cabbage, carrots, onions and pumpkin in autumn; rhubarb and strawberries in June, plums in August, apples and pears in autumn. Plan about five weeks of active work over two to three months, following the harvest; the ferments and the confit run in the background.

**Have ready:** a 2-litre preserving jar or crock with a weight (a plate and a water-filled bag will do); preserving jars with new two-piece lids; a deep pot with a rack or a folded tea towel under the jars; a jar lifter and a wide funnel; the 1 g scale and, if a tested cure needs curing salt, the 0.01 g scale; a room thermometer; pH strips (optional); a heavy saucepan; labels and a marker; non-iodised salt; the processing log; the pantry inventory; the journal.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `PRS-3.M1` in the course file, 5 of them safety items. Pass mark 80 %, with every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** every preserve here is safe because a few hurdles together stop the organisms that matter. Knowing them tells you what you may change in a recipe and what you may not.
**You need:** the hurdle table below; a few preserving recipes; the NCHFP site [S27]; the journal.
**Explanation:**
*The hurdles.* Each method takes away one or more things microbes need:

rows: Acid (pH 4.6 or below), heat, a sealed jar
Salt, then the acid the bacteria make, no air
Sugar, acid, heat, a sealed jar
Cupboard if processed; fridge once opened

blocks.text: *Why combinations matter.* One hurdle alone is often not enough; together they hold. Removing one (less vinegar, sugar or salt) can break the combination, though the jar looks the same.

*What only a tested method can make safe.* *Clostridium botulinum* grows without air in moist, low-acid food, and its toxin gives no warning. Foods above pH 4.6 are low-acid: meat, fish, milk and all fresh vegetables except most tomatoes (§9). A boiling-water bath is enough only for acid foods; low-acid foods need pressure canning, which the program does not teach (§9). So a tested method is needed for:

items.text: anything canned;
low-acid foods kept without the fridge;
garlic, herbs or vegetables kept in oil;
cured meats eaten without cooking.

blocks.text: *Recognising an untested or unsafe recipe.* Ask seven questions:

items.text: Is the source an authority that tested it (NCHFP or equivalent), or does it name one?
Does a canned recipe give a processing time and a jar size?
Is a low-acid food being water-bath canned?
Does it say "to taste" for vinegar, sugar or salt where they are hurdles?
Is something kept in oil at room temperature?
Does it use oven canning, open-kettle canning (filled hot and sealed without processing) or a wax seal?
Does a cure for meat eaten raw lack a nitrite dose (§9)?

blocks.text: **Practice:** theory only (2 h): for each preserve you plan to make, write its hurdles and whether it needs a tested method; then read three recipes against the seven questions, as the warm-up for `PRS-3.M1.X1`.
**Look for:** for any preserve, you name its hurdles without the table, and whether it needs a tested recipe.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Ask the seven questions; a habit that worked is not a tested method
Halving the sugar in a canned jam
Sugar is a hurdle; choose a tested low-sugar recipe, or keep the jam in the fridge
Oil keeps air out, which botulism likes; keep it in the fridge (§9)
Beans taken for an acid food
Beans are low-acid; pickle them by a tested recipe, or freeze them

blocks.text: **Safety:** a preserve without a tested method is refused or replaced by a tested one; a doubtful jar is thrown away unopened (`SAF-3.M1.L3`).
**Record:** the hurdles of each planned preserve, and the tested source you will use for it.

items.question: Which may be canned in a boiling-water bath?

options.text: a pickle from a tested recipe with enough vinegar to be an acid food

items.why: Acid foods only (pH 4.6 or below), by a tested recipe (§9).

items.question: A canned chutney recipe says "add vinegar to taste". What is wrong?

options.text: vinegar is a hurdle: a canned recipe must state it, so the recipe is untested

items.why: Hurdles are not "to taste" in canned recipes.

items.question: What keeps sauerkraut safe?

options.text: salt, then the lactic acid the bacteria make, without air

items.question: What is open-kettle canning?

options.text: filling jars hot and sealing without processing: unsafe

items.question: Why does halving the sugar in a jam recipe matter?

options.text: sugar is a hurdle; less sugar means more free water, so it keeps less well and must be refrigerated or frozen

items.question: Which needs a tested method most?

options.text: a fridge pickle eaten this week
a jar of vegetables kept in the cupboard

items.question: A friend's recipe stores roasted peppers and garlic in olive oil in the cupboard for months. What do you tell them?
items.answer: It is unsafe: vegetables and garlic in oil are low-acid and without air, a botulism risk. Keep it in the fridge and use it soon, or freeze it, or use a tested acidified recipe.

a cooking video without a source

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `PRS-3.M2` in the course file, 5 of them safety items. Pass mark 80 %, with every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a quick pickle is the fastest preserve there is, ready in hours, and the easiest way to bring acid and crunch to a plate. It is also the base on which water-bath canning builds.

**You need:** red onions, pickling cucumbers and one more vegetable in season; white wine or cider vinegar of 5 % acidity; water; non-iodised salt; sugar; mustard seed, dill, bay, chilli, peppercorns, juniper or fennel seed; clean jars with lids; a saucepan; the scale; labels; the tasting form.
**Explanation:**
*A quick (fridge) pickle* is vegetables in a hot or cold brine of vinegar, water, salt and sugar, kept in the fridge. It is not processed, so it is not shelf-stable: the fridge is one of its hurdles.

*The brine.* No NCHFP recipe is written for the fridge, so the program borrows the pickling solution of NCHFP's *Quick Fresh-Pack Dill Pickles* [S27]: 1.5 quarts of 5 % vinegar to 2 quarts of water, which is **3 parts vinegar to 4 parts water by volume**. That is the floor: more vinegar is allowed, more water never, and vinegar of unknown or lower acidity is never used (NCHFP: "do not alter vinegar, food, or water proportions") [S27]. Salt and sugar are flavour here, weighed against the liquid: a starting point is about 4 % salt and 1.5 % sugar, converted from the recipe's half cup of salt and quarter cup of sugar. For a 700 ml brine: 300 ml vinegar, 400 ml water, 28 g salt, 10 g sugar.

*Varying the aromatics.* Mustard seed, dill, bay, chilli, garlic, peppercorns, juniper or fennel seed; the acid as wine, cider or rice vinegar of the same 5 %; sugar up for sweet-sour, down for sharp. What changes is flavour; the vinegar-to-water floor stays.

*The vegetables.* Firm and fresh: cucumbers, beans, carrots, red onions, beetroot, radishes, cauliflower and courgettes in summer; cabbage and roots in winter. Cut them evenly and pack them tight, so the brine covers everything.

*The method.* Bring the brine to the boil with the salt, sugar and spices. Pack the vegetables into hot-washed jars. Pour the hot brine over to cover, close the jar, cool it, and put it in the fridge. Red onions are ready in an hour; cucumbers taste best after a day.

*Jars.* Clean, hot-washed, labelled with the content and the date. A fridge pickle keeps its crunch for some weeks, but no tested keeping time exists for it; you set a use-by date for quality in your inventory (`PRS-3.M6.L1`).
**Practice:**

items.text: **Two quick pickles (60 min).** Red onions and cucumbers in a hot brine by the ratio, weighed; tasted after an hour and after a day.
**A third with varied aromatics (45 min).** A seasonal vegetable with different spices and acid; compared with the first two on the form.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: crisp after a day;
sour, salt and sweet in balance;
every jar labelled and dated.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Never below 3 parts vinegar to 4 parts water; start again
Cooked in the brine, or old produce
Pour the brine over raw, fresh vegetables
Label every jar as you fill it

blocks.text: **Safety:** quick pickles live in the fridge at 4 °C, never in the cupboard. Mustard is an allergen (`SAF-1.M4`): label a pickle that contains mustard seed.
**Record:** the brine weighed, the three pickles, and the tastings after an hour and a day.
**Why it matters:** a sealed jar on the shelf has only its acid and its seal between it and botulism, so every step of the tested recipe matters. Done exactly, it is simple; changed, it is guesswork.

**You need:** the tested recipe of `PRS-3.M2.X2` printed; preserving jars with new two-piece lids; a deep pot with a rack (or a folded tea towel) so the jars sit off the bottom; a jar lifter; a wide funnel; a ruler for headspace; US measuring cups and spoons (NCHFP recipes use them); a timer; labels; the processing log.
**Explanation:**
*When.* Only acid foods, at pH 4.6 or below, by a tested recipe and its processing time, followed exactly; low-acid foods need pressure canning, which the program does not teach (§9).
*The steps of a tested recipe:*

items.text: jars washed and kept hot;
food prepared exactly as written: the cut, the amounts, the vinegar strength;
jars filled to the stated **headspace** (the gap between the food and the lid), air bubbles released with a clean spatula, rims wiped;
lids on, bands finger-tight;
processed in boiling water for the stated time, **timed from when the water returns to the boil**, with the jars covered by water as the recipe says;
lifted out upright and left undisturbed to cool.

blocks.text: Measure in the recipe's US cups and spoons; use its 0–1,000 ft time.
*The seal check (NCHFP)* [S27]. Cool the jars at room temperature for 12 to 24 hours; do not retighten the lids. Then take off the bands and test:

items.text: press the centre of the lid: if it springs up when you release it, it is not sealed;
or tap it with a teaspoon: a ringing note means sealed, a dull one not;
or look across it: a sealed lid curves down.

blocks.text: A jar that didn't seal goes into the fridge and is eaten within several days, or is reprocessed within 24 hours with the same time.

*Storage (NCHFP)* [S27]: labelled and dated; in a clean, cool, dark, dry place, best at 10–21 °C, never above 35 °C, near a stove or in sunlight; stored without the bands; used within a year for best quality.
*Spoiled jars.* A bulging lid, a broken seal, spurting liquid, mould or an odd smell: **do not taste it** (NCHFP). Throw the jar away unopened, sealed in a heavy bin bag (`SAF-3.M1.L3`).
*Not recommended (NCHFP)* [S27]: open-kettle canning (filled hot, sealed, not processed), and jars processed in an oven, microwave or dishwasher. Nor does the program use wax seals.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A canned pickle (2 h).** The pickled beetroot of `PRS-3.M2.X2`, processed by its tested recipe; the seals checked and logged the next day.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the headspace measured, the time counted from the return to the boil;
every lid sealed and curved down after a day.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Timer started when the jars went in
Start it when the water boils again
Old flat lids reused, or a rim not wiped
New lids every time; wipe each rim
Jars that leak or don't seal
Fill to the stated headspace, no more
Never taste it; throw it away sealed

blocks.text: **Safety:** acid foods and tested recipes only; hot jars moved upright with the lifter; a doubtful jar never tasted.
**Record:** the processing log: recipe and URL, headspace, the time from the return to the boil, and the seal check.

In the fridge, labelled and dated

Make the three pickles; vary the aromatics; change the sugar in one.

exercises.title: A water-bath-canned pickle from a tested recipe
exercises.description: One water-bath-canned pickle from a tested recipe.

blocks.text: **Task:** can an acid pickle exactly by a tested recipe, with every control point logged. The recipe is NCHFP's *Pickled Beets* (nchfp.uga.edu, Pickling, Vegetable pickles) [S27], followed exactly in its US measures: beetroot is Dutch and in season from late summer. Keep the processing log, label the jars, and open one after a month.

**You need:** about 3.2 kg (7 lb) of small beetroot, 5–6 cm across; 4 cups of 5 % vinegar; 2 cups of water; 2 cups of sugar; 1.5 teaspoons of canning or non-iodised salt; 2 cinnamon sticks; 12 cloves; onions if wanted, as the page says; about eight pint jars (about 0.5 l) with new lids; the deep pot with a rack; the jar lifter; the funnel; a ruler.
**Recipe:** pickled beetroot (NCHFP).

items.text: **Read** the page and copy its control points into the log: headspace ½ inch (about 1.25 cm), hot pack, pints or quarts, 30 minutes at 0–1,000 ft.
**Cook** the beetroot until tender, about 25 to 30 minutes; discard that liquid; peel and slice ¼ inch (about 6 mm).
**Simmer** the beetroot (and onions) for 5 minutes in the vinegar, water, sugar and salt, with the spices in a bag, then remove the bag.
**Fill** the hot jars, leaving ½ inch headspace with the hot liquid; release bubbles; wipe the rims; lids on.
**Process** for 30 minutes from the return to the boil; log the clock times.
**Cool** undisturbed for 12 to 24 hours; take off the bands; check and log every seal; refrigerate any jar that didn't seal.
**Store** labelled with the content, the date and the source; open one jar after a month and judge it.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`TS-PRS` level 3, further evidence:** a canned pickle by a tested method, labelled, judged after storage.
**`SA-HRPR` level 4, further evidence:** a canning plan with control points, followed in the log, the tested source named.

blocks.text: AI review reads the log and the photos: *competent* is every control point with its figure, the time from the return to the boil, and a seal result per jar; *not yet* is a missing time or headspace, or a change to the recipe.
**Time:** 2 h, plus the check after a day.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `PRS-3.M3` in the course file, 4 of them safety items. Pass mark 80 %, with every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** sauerkraut is the Dutch preserve of the cabbage harvest, and the clearest example of a ferment: you add only salt, and the bacteria make the acid that keeps it. Get the salt and the temperature right, and the rest follows.

**You need:** about 2 kg of white cabbage (autumn); non-iodised salt; a 2-litre preserving jar or crock; a weight (a plate and a water-filled bag, or glass weights); a large bowl; the 1 g scale; a room thermometer; the fermentation log.
**Explanation:**

*Salt by weight* (§9, [S36]): **2.25–2.5 % of the shredded cabbage's weight**, weighed, never measured by the spoon. For 2,000 g of cabbage, that is 45–50 g of salt. Too little salt softens the kraut; too much slows the fermentation and can turn it pink. Use non-iodised salt.

*Packing and weighting.* Remove the outer leaves and the core; shred the cabbage finely and weigh it. Mix it with the salt and leave it for 10 minutes, then squeeze and press it hard, in handfuls, into the jar, until its own juice rises and covers it. Keep it under the brine with a weight. Air is kept out: the cabbage stays submerged.
*Temperature and time* (§9, [S27]):

items.text: at 21–24 °C, about 3–4 weeks;
at 16–18 °C, 5–6 weeks;
below about 16 °C it may not ferment; above about 24 °C it can turn soft.

blocks.text: Put the jar where the room thermometer shows the right range: not beside the heating. A dish under the jar catches any overflow.

*The bacterial succession.* First, salt-tolerant bacteria (*Leuconostoc*) make gas and some acid. As the acid builds, *Lactobacillus* species take over and bring the pH lower. The acid and the salt together keep spoilage organisms and pathogens out.
*Reading it daily.* Look at the brine level (topped up if it falls), the bubbling, the surface and the smell, and log each. Bubbles appear in the first days; the smell turns cleanly sour.
*Done.* The bubbling has stopped and the flavour is pleasantly sour. Fully fermented kraut keeps for several months in the fridge, tightly covered [S27].
**Practice:**

items.text: **Make it (60 min, then weeks).** The sauerkraut of `PRS-3.M3.X1`: weighed, salted, packed and weighted; the log started with the cabbage weight, the salt weight and the room temperature.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: brine above the cabbage;
bubbles in the first days;
a clean, sour smell.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Too little salt, or too warm
Weigh the salt; move the jar to 21–24 °C or lower
Press harder; weigh it down; add brine at the same salt %
Move it somewhere warmer within the range

blocks.text: **Safety:** the salt is weighed to the §9 percentage; the cabbage stays under the brine; mould means the ferment is thrown away (`PRS-3.M3.L2`).
**Record:** the cabbage and salt weights, the salt %, the room temperature, and the daily log.
**Why it matters:** a ferment changes daily, and most of what you see is normal. Telling normal from spoiled, and kahm yeast from mould, saves good ferments and throws away the dangerous ones.

**You need:** a Chinese or savoy cabbage; radishes or carrots; spring onions; garlic; ginger; chilli flakes; fish sauce or soy sauce; non-iodised salt; a jar with a weight; gloves for the chilli; the scale; the log; eight ferment photos (from the course's photo set or your own).
**Explanation:**

*A kimchi-style mixed ferment.* Salt the cabbage pieces by weight and leave them until limp; rinse and drain them. Mix them with a paste of chilli, garlic, ginger and spring onion, and fish sauce or soy sauce, and with carrots or radishes. Pack it tightly into the jar, pressed under its own liquid. Leave it at room temperature until it bubbles and smells sour, logging it daily, then keep it in the fridge. Dutch cabbage, radishes and spring onions suit it. It has no tested NCHFP recipe, so it is a fridge ferment, not a cupboard one.
*Brine ferments.* Whole or cut vegetables (cucumbers, carrots, beans) are fermented in a weighed brine, at the brine strength a tested recipe gives [S27], kept under it.
*Normal or spoiled:*

items.text: **normal:** bubbling, cloudy brine, a sour smell, a little white sediment at the bottom;
**kahm yeast:** a flat, white, wrinkled film on the surface. Harmless but off-tasting: skim it off; the vegetables under the brine are fine;
**mould:** fuzzy, raised spots, green, black, pink or blue. **Discard the whole ferment**: never scrape it off;
**spoiled:** slimy or soft vegetables, a rotten or putrid smell, pink or dark discoloured kraut. **Discard it.**

blocks.text: *When in doubt, throw it out.* Then change the salt, the weight or the temperature next time, and note why.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A mixed ferment (60 min, then two weeks).** A kimchi-style ferment packed and logged daily.
**Diagnose (30 min).** Eight ferment photos (normal, kahm yeast, mould, spoiled), each judged and the action written.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: you name kahm yeast and mould from photos, and say what to do;
the log shows the day the ferment went into the fridge, and why.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Scraped off "and the rest is fine"
A little kahm yeast taken for mould
Flat and white is yeast: skim it
Slimy or putrid is thrown away untasted

blocks.text: **Safety:** fish sauce is a fish allergen, soy a soy allergen, and chilli is handled with gloves (`SAF-1.M4`); label the jar. A doubtful ferment is never tasted.
**Record:** the kimchi log, and the eight diagnoses with their actions.

exercises.title: Sauerkraut by percentage, with a daily log
exercises.description: Sauerkraut by percentage, with a daily log.

blocks.text: **Task:** ferment sauerkraut by a weighed salt percentage, and read its progress by cues before checking. Ferment about 2 kg of cabbage at a weighed 2.25–2.5 % salt, kept under the brine, at a logged room temperature. Keep a daily log of cues. From the second week, write your prediction of "done" before each check, then taste (and, optionally, read a pH strip). Label the kraut, and judge it after a month in the fridge.
**You need:** about 2 kg of Dutch white cabbage (autumn); non-iodised salt; a fermentation jar or crock with a weight; a room thermometer; pH strips (optional); the scale; the daily log.
**Framework:** the ferment.

rows: 2.25–2.5 % of the shredded cabbage's weight, weighed (§9)
Pressed until the juice covers it, weighted, no air
From week 2: predict "done", then taste or pH strip
Bubbling stopped, pleasantly sour; to the fridge, labelled
Mould, slime, a putrid smell, pink or dark kraut

blocks.text: *Procedure:*

items.text: Weigh the shredded cabbage; calculate and weigh the salt; log both.
Pack and weight; log the room temperature.
Log the cues daily; from the second week, predict, then check.
Judge it done; move it to the fridge; label it.
Judge its quality after a month.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`TS-PRS` level 3, the lacto-ferment part:** a ferment at a weighed salt percentage with a daily log, by a tested method, labelled, judged on quality after storage.
**`JD-CUES` level 4, further evidence:** cue-then-check entries in an unfamiliar situation (the predicted state of the ferment against the taste or pH reading).

blocks.text: AI review reads the log and the photos: *competent* is a salt within 2.25–2.5 %, the brine above the cabbage in every photo, and predictions written before each check; *not yet* is salt by the spoon, a gap of days in the log, or a mouldy ferment kept.
**Time:** 1 h, plus a few minutes a day for 3–6 weeks.

At what room temperature does sauerkraut ferment in about 3–4 weeks?
Which bacteria take over as the acid builds?
Too much salt in sauerkraut:

options.text: slows the fermentation and can turn it pink

items.question: Photo: a flat, white, wrinkled film on the brine of a ferment. What is it, and what do you do?
items.answer: Kahm yeast: skim it off; the vegetables under the brine are fine.

items.question: Photo: fuzzy green and black spots on top of a ferment. What do you do?
items.answer: Discard the whole ferment: it is mould.

items.question: A ferment is slimy and smells rotten. What do you do?
Why is the cabbage kept under the brine?

options.text: to keep air out so moulds can't grow and the right bacteria thrive

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `PRS-3.M4` in the course file, 5 of them safety items. Pass mark 80 %, with every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a cure turns pork belly into your own bacon, seasoned through. Curing by weight makes it repeatable; knowing when nitrite is needed keeps it safe.

**You need:** a piece of pork belly of about 1 kg, skin on or off; non-iodised salt; sugar; black pepper, juniper, bay and thyme; a freezer bag or a covered container that fits it; the 1 g scale; the curing log; labels.
**Explanation:**

*Equilibrium curing.* Weigh the meat; weigh the salt and sugar as a percentage of that weight; seal them with the meat in a bag in the fridge. The meat takes up all of that salt and no more, so given enough time it reaches the same salt level throughout and can never be over-salted. A starting point is **2.5 % salt and 1 % sugar** by the meat's weight: for a 1,000 g belly, 25 g salt and 10 g sugar. This is a quality choice, not a safety figure: the safety comes from the fridge and the cooking. Log the percentage you use and adjust it to taste next time.

*The cure.* Rub the salt, sugar and crushed aromatics over the meat; seal it in the bag with the air pressed out. Keep it in the fridge at 4 °C for about a week, turning it daily, so the liquid that forms reaches every side. The belly is ready when it feels firm throughout. Rinse it, dry it, and cook it. A duck breast can be cured the same way and then cooked.
*Cooking it.* The program's cures are cooked before eating:

items.text: pork belly as intact meat to 63 °C for 15 seconds at the core (§9), whether roasted or sliced and fried;
a cured duck breast as poultry, to 75 °C (§9).

blocks.text: Uncooked, it stays in the fridge for the cure time; cooked, it keeps as leftovers (2 days) or is frozen.
*When nitrite is needed, and the dose* (§9, `SAF-3.M1.L3`):

items.text: **needed** for meat eaten without cooking or kept long: air-dried hams, cold-smoked meat, fermented sausages;
**not needed** for the program's cures, which are cooked before eating and kept in the fridge;
where a tested recipe calls for nitrite curing salt, the added nitrite stays at **80 mg per kg of meat or below**, as the nitrite ion, calculated from the label and weighed on a 0.01 g scale.

blocks.text: An example label: 0.5 % sodium nitrite. Sodium nitrite is about two-thirds nitrite ion by weight (46 of 69), so 80 mg of nitrite ion is 120 mg of sodium nitrite: at most 24 g of that salt per kg of meat. Your own label changes the arithmetic.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A cure by weight (45 min, then about a week).** The pork belly weighed, the cure weighed by percentage and logged, turned daily, and cooked at the end of the cure time.

blocks.text: **Look for:** every weight in the log, with the percentage; the meat firm and evenly seasoned when cooked.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Weigh the meat and the cure; log the %
Curing salt where none is needed
Plain salt for a cooked cure
Cook it to its §9 figure first

blocks.text: **Safety:** a cured belly is raw meat: stored in the fridge on the bottom shelf, cooked to its §9 figure, its board and knife treated as raw meat's.
**Record:** the meat weight, the cure weights and %, the days, and the cooked result.

**Why it matters:** confit is cooking slowly under fat, the old way to keep duck legs. The cooking still works; the keeping does not, without the fridge. This lesson keeps the first and changes the second.
**You need:** two heads of garlic; a neutral oil or duck fat; a small saucepan; a clean jar; labels; the probe. For the explanation: the duck legs of `BUT-3.M1.X1` (cooked in `PRS-3.M4.X1`).
**Explanation:**

*Duck confit.* Salt the legs by weight (the starting point of `PRS-3.M4.L1`), overnight in the fridge. Rinse and dry them; submerge them in duck fat; cook them in a low oven, the fat barely trembling, until a skewer slides into the thigh with no resistance. The core passes 75 °C (the poultry row of §9) long before the meat is tender. Cool them in the fat.

*Garlic confit.* Peel the cloves; cover them with oil in a small pan; cook them very gently, with only small bubbles, until they are soft and golden, not brown. Garlic in oil is a botulism risk (§9): keep it in the fridge and use it within 2 days, or freeze it.
*Safe storage in fat:*

items.text: fat keeps out air, and *C. botulinum* grows without air, so the fat is not a safety hurdle on its own;

confit is cooled by the standard (57 °C to 21 °C within 2 hours, and to 5 °C or below within 6 hours in total, §9), kept covered in its fat in the fridge, and used within 2 days, or frozen in its fat for longer;
the traditional months under fat in a cellar have no checked figure and are not taught;
the strained fat is reused for potatoes and further confit, kept in the fridge.

blocks.text: *Serving.* Crisp the legs skin-side down in a hot pan or oven until they are steaming hot throughout (§9). Serve them with potatoes cooked in the fat and something sharp: a pickle, a chicory salad.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Garlic confit (30 min active, 1 h in total).** A small batch, cooled, labelled and refrigerated; used within 2 days, on toast, in a dressing or mashed into potatoes.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the garlic soft and golden, not brown;
the oil never more than gently bubbling;
the jar dated and in the fridge.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: In the fridge, within 2 days, or frozen
Confit kept for weeks in the fridge
2 days in the fridge; freeze it for longer
Lower the heat: small bubbles only

blocks.text: **Safety:** hot fat and oil are handled with dry tools and the pan kept stable; garlic in oil and confit are always refrigerated or frozen (§9).
**Record:** the garlic batch, the date made and the day used.

exercises.title: Duck leg confit, stored and used two weeks later
exercises.description: Duck legs confit (from `BUT-3`), stored and used two weeks later.

blocks.text: **Task:** confit the two duck legs from `BUT-3`, store them safely, and judge their quality two weeks later. Salt them by weight overnight, and log the cure. Cook them submerged in fat until tender, cool them by the standard, and freeze them in their fat, labelled: freezing is the program's rule for storage beyond 2 days. Two weeks later, thaw them in the fridge, crisp them, and judge their quality on the form.

**You need:** the two duck legs of `BUT-3.M1.X1`; salt; thyme; garlic; the rendered duck fat, topped up with bought duck fat if needed; an ovenproof dish that fits the legs snugly; the probe; a freezer container; labels; the scale; the log.
**Framework:** the confit.

rows: Salt by weight (start at 2.5 %), thyme, garlic, overnight in the fridge
Submerged in fat, in a low oven, fat barely trembling, until tender
57 °C to 21 °C within 2 h, to 5 °C within 6 h in total
Frozen in its fat, labelled with content and date
Thawed in the fridge; crisped until steaming hot throughout

blocks.text: *Procedure:*

items.text: Weigh the legs; weigh and log the salt; cure overnight in the fridge.
Rinse, dry and confit; log the oven setting and the time.
Cool by the standard; freeze in the fat; label.
Two weeks later: thaw in the fridge, crisp, serve; judge the quality.

blocks.text: **Show:** the cure part of the `TS-PRS` level 3 row: a cure by weight logged, a confit by a tested method, labelled, judged on quality after two weeks' storage. The ferment and the sugar preserve are in `PRS-3.M3.X1` and `PRS-3.M5.X1`.

AI review reads the log and the photos: *competent* is the cure weighed, the cooling times logged, a frozen, labelled confit and crisp skin two weeks later; *not yet* is confit kept in the fridge for the two weeks, or no cooling record.
**Time:** 1.5 h active over two days, plus the serving.

items.question: Why can't an equilibrium cure over-salt the meat?

options.text: the salt is a set percentage of the meat's weight, which it reaches throughout

items.question: When is nitrite curing salt needed?

options.text: for meat eaten without cooking or kept long, such as air-dried hams and fermented sausages

items.question: A curing salt contains 0.6 % sodium nitrite. Roughly how much nitrite ion is added per kg of meat with 20 g of this salt? (Sodium nitrite × 0.67 = nitrite ion.)
items.answer: About 80 mg (20 g × 0.006 = 120 mg sodium nitrite; × 0.67 ≈ 80 mg)

items.question: Your pork belly has been cured with plain salt. How is it eaten?
items.why: No nitrite, so it is cooked.

items.question: How long is duck confit kept in the fridge in this program?

options.text: at most 2 days; frozen in its fat for longer

items.why: §9 leftovers rule; no checked longer figure.

items.question: Garlic confit in oil is stored:

options.text: in the fridge and used within 2 days, or frozen

items.question: Why does fat not make confit safe on its own?

options.text: it keeps air out, which botulism bacteria like; cold and cooking are the hurdles

items.question: How is the skin of a confit leg crisped?

options.text: skin-side down in a hot pan or in a hot oven

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** drying is the oldest hurdle and needs no additives: take away the water and microbes cannot grow. A home oven does it slowly; the skill is in knowing when the food is dry, and keeping it that way.

**You need:** woody herbs (thyme, rosemary, sage); ripe Dutch tomatoes (late summer); mushrooms; apples or pears; a lemon or vinegar for acidulated water; oven racks or wire racks on trays; a wooden spoon to hold the door ajar; clean, dry jars; the scale; labels; the log.
**Explanation:**
*Water activity.* Microbes need free water; drying removes it until they cannot grow. The food is dry when it is leathery or brittle, by type, with no moist centre.

*The low oven.* The lowest setting, often 50–70 °C, with the door slightly ajar so the moisture can escape; the food in a single layer on a rack, with air around every piece. A dehydrator does the same job; NCHFP describes dehydrators as designed to dry foods fast at 60 °C (140 °F) [S27]. An oven that runs hotter cooks the food instead of drying it.
*What dries well at home:*

items.text: **herbs,** woody ones best: air-dried in bunches or on a rack, or in the oven at its lowest; dry when they crumble;
**tomatoes,** halved and seasoned: leathery, with no moist centre;
**mushrooms,** sliced: dried until brittle;
**apple and pear rings,** dipped in acidulated water against browning: leathery and pliable.

blocks.text: *When it is dry (NCHFP)* [S27]. Vegetables are dried until they are brittle or crisp. Fruit stays leathery, with about 20 % moisture, so it is **conditioned**: cooled, packed loosely in jars, sealed and left for 7 to 10 days, shaken daily. If condensation appears, the fruit goes back for more drying.

*Storage (NCHFP)* [S27]. Cooled completely first, then in clean, dry jars or freezer containers with tight lids, in a cool, dark, dry place, labelled. Most dried fruit keeps about a year stored cool, about half that stored warm; vegetables keep about half as long as fruit. Dried tomatoes or herbs put into oil become an oil preserve: in the fridge, and used within 2 days (§9).
*Weighing.* Weigh the food before and after: the loss is the water removed, and the record tells you next time how far to take it.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A drying session (90 min active, a day in total).** Herbs, tomatoes and apple rings, weighed before and after; stored, and checked after three days for condensation.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: no moisture in the centre when a piece is torn;
no condensation in the jar after three days.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: The oven too hot, the door shut
The lowest setting, the door ajar
Packed warm, or not dry enough
Cool completely; back into the oven
Dried tomatoes in oil on the shelf

blocks.text: **Safety:** a door held ajar leaves a hot oven open: keep children and tea towels away, and switch the oven off when you leave the house. Dried food in oil is kept in the fridge (§9).
**Record:** the weights before and after, the oven setting and time, and the condensation check.
**Why it matters:** in jam, sugar is a hurdle and a texture at once; in chutney, vegetables meet vinegar and sugar. Both use the gluts of the Dutch summer and autumn.

**You need:** seasonal fruit (plums in August, apples in autumn); powdered pectin if the tested recipe needs it; sugar; cider vinegar of 5 %; onions; spices; a wide, heavy pan; saucers in the freezer; the thermometer; preserving jars with new lids; the deep pot with a rack; US measuring cups; labels; red onions for the comparison.
**Explanation:**

*How a jam sets.* Pectin from the fruit, sugar and acid together form a gel when the mixture is boiled to the setting point. High-pectin fruit (apples, plums, redcurrants, citrus peel) sets easily; low-pectin fruit (strawberries, rhubarb, pears) needs added pectin, lemon juice, or a high-pectin fruit mixed in.

*Vegetable pectin.* Vegetables have pectin too, which is why a chutney thickens as it reduces. Acid keeps vegetables firm and sets their colour: red onion and red cabbage turn bright pink with acid (`VEG-1.M1` compared carrots in acid and alkali).
*The set test.*

items.text: **with added pectin:** the tested recipe's boil (for NCHFP's plum jam, a full rolling boil, then a hard boil for one minute after the sugar) is the set; follow it exactly;
**without added pectin:** a spoonful on a saucer from the freezer wrinkles when pushed after a few minutes; or the temperature the tested recipe gives, on the thermometer.

blocks.text: *Sugar is a hurdle* (`PRS-3.M1`). A full-sugar jam by a tested recipe, water-bath processed, keeps in the cupboard until opened; opened, it goes in the fridge and is best within a month (NCHFP) [S27]. Sweeteners are not substituted for the sugar in a regular-pectin recipe; low-sugar spreads use a tested low-sugar recipe and its pectin, or are kept in the fridge or freezer.
*Marmalade.* Citrus peel, pith and juice cooked long; the peel's pectin sets it. Citrus is imported, so marmalade is taught as a method and is optional, with Seville oranges in January.

*Chutney.* Fruit or vegetables with vinegar, sugar and spices, cooked down until a spoon drawn across the pan leaves a channel. It mellows after a few weeks. It is canned only by a tested recipe, otherwise kept in the fridge.

*Seasonal choices.* Rhubarb and strawberry in June, plums in August, apples and pears in autumn; pumpkin, beetroot, red onion or green tomato chutney in autumn, in the fridge unless a tested recipe exists.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A jam (75 min).** The plum jam of `PRS-3.M5.X1` by its tested recipe; the set checked on a cold saucer; jarred and processed.
**A chutney (90 min).** The apple chutney of `PRS-3.M5.X1`, cooked to a channel and jarred; a red onion cooked with and without vinegar, photographed side by side for colour.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: a set that wrinkles on the cold saucer;
a chutney that holds a channel;
every jar labelled.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Follow the tested boil; test early
Sugar halved in a canned recipe
A tested low-sugar recipe, or the fridge
Cook on until a spoon leaves a channel

blocks.text: **Safety:** boiling jam is hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin: a deep pan, long sleeves, a long spoon, and children away. Mustard seed is an allergen (`SAF-1.M4`): label the chutney.
**Record:** the set test, the processing log, and the onion photos.

blocks.text: **Task:** make a set jam and a chutney from seasonal produce by tested recipes; process, label and judge one jar of each after a month. Then cook red onion with and without vinegar, or with a pinch of baking soda, and explain in writing what heat, acid and alkali do to colour and texture.

**You need:** for the jam, NCHFP's *Plum Jam with Powdered Pectin* [S27]: 6 cups crushed plums (about 1.6 kg, 3.5 lb), one package of powdered pectin, 8 cups of sugar (about nine half-pint jars). Dutch *geleisuiker* is a different product and is no substitute. For the chutney, NCHFP's *Apple Chutney* [S27] in its US measures, with tart Dutch apples (about six pints). Red onions and baking soda; jars with new lids; the deep pot; labels.
**Framework:** the two tested ratios.

rows: Plums, pectin, sugar exactly as written; a full boil, sugar in, a hard boil for 1 minute
¼ inch headspace; 5 minutes' processing at 0–1,000 ft
The tested amounts; simmered until thick (about 45 minutes) and a spoon leaves a channel
Pints, ½ inch headspace; 10 minutes' processing at 0–1,000 ft
Cooled undisturbed 12–24 h; seals checked and logged
Into the fridge; jam best within a month

items.text: Measure by the recipe; cook the jam to the set; jar it.
Cook the chutney to a channel; jar it.
Process both by the tested times; cool; check the seals; label.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** none for this module. It has no knowledge or judgment objective; the storage rules were checked in `PRS-3.M1` to `PRS-3.M5`.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a pantry no one uses is waste in jars. Preserves earn their place as ingredients that bring acid, crunch, depth and sweetness to weeknight cooking, and an inventory keeps them used in time.
**You need:** every preserve you have made in this course; the pantry inventory (a list or a spreadsheet); labels and a marker; seasonal produce for a weeknight meal.
**Explanation:**
*Preserves as ingredients:*

items.text: pickles and their brine as acid and crunch (`FLV-3.M3`): a spoonful of brine in a dressing or a sauce;
sauerkraut in a *stamppot*, a soup or a braise, or raw as a salad;
confit as a quick main;
dried mushrooms and tomatoes as umami in a stock, a sauce or a braise;
jam in a glaze, a sauce or a dessert;
chutney with cheese and cold meat.

blocks.text: *The inventory.* Every jar is listed with its content, the date made, the storage method and container, and a use-by date chosen for quality as well as safety: the tested method's limit, or earlier when quality fades. Some limits from the course:

items.text: canned jars: within a year for best quality (NCHFP) [S27];
opened full-sugar jam: in the fridge, best within a month (NCHFP);
sauerkraut: several months in the fridge, covered [S27];
garlic confit and preserves in oil: 2 days in the fridge (§9);
confit: 2 days in the fridge, or frozen;
quick pickles and frozen confit: your own quality date, set on tasting.

blocks.text: Check the inventory monthly: first in, first out.
*Labels.* Content and date; for canned jars, the tested source too. An opened jar is dated again and moved to the fridge.
*Using up surplus.* The preserves come from gluts, trim and leftovers (stems into pickles, peel into chutney), which is where they save waste.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The inventory (45 min).** List every preserve; check the labels; fix the storage; set the use-by dates.
**A weeknight meal from the pantry (60 min).** A dinner built around two preserves, for example a *stamppot* of sauerkraut with crisped bacon from `PRS-3.M4.L1`, and pickled beetroot on the side.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: an inventory that matches the shelves;
nothing past its date;
opened jars in the fridge.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Label as you fill; if unknown, throw it out
An old opened jar at the back of the fridge
Plan one preserve into each week's menu

blocks.text: **Safety:** a jar you cannot identify or date is thrown away; a canned jar with a doubtful seal is never tasted.
**Record:** the inventory, and the meal with its two preserves.

exercises.title: A dinner in which each course uses a preserve
exercises.description: A dinner in which each course uses one of your preserves.

blocks.text: **Task:** cook a dinner for guests from the pantry you have built, and keep the pantry for quality.

items.text: **The brief:** a three-course dinner for guests in which each course uses one of your preserves.
**The constraints:**
the inventory of `PRS-3.M6.L1` kept up to date, with the storage method, container, label and a quality use-by date per item;
the dinner logged with the control-point plan of `SAF-3.M2.X1`;
allergens and risk groups asked about in advance.
**The criteria:** the quality of each preserve noted on the day of use; the week's food waste logged by weight, with the surplus and trim the preserves used.
**The record:** the menu, the inventory, the quality notes, the waste log, guest cards and your review.

blocks.text: **You need:** the preserves of the course; seasonal produce for the rest of the dinner; the inventory; the scale; the control-point plan; guest cards.
**Show:**

items.text: **`IN-STO` level 4:** every preserve with a storage method, container, label and use-by date chosen for quality as well as safety; on the day of use, the quality notes show nothing lost to storage. With the spice plan of `FLV-3.M2.X2` and the freezer plan of `KMG-3.M4.X1`, the row is met for every kind of storage.
**`KM-WAST` level 4, further evidence:** surplus and trim preserved and used, edible waste logged under 5 % by weight.
The dinner's log also counts as one of the productions of `SA-HYG` level 5 (`SAF-3.M2.X1`).

blocks.text: AI review reads the inventory, the notes and the waste log: *competent* is a complete inventory, quality notes for all three preserves and waste under 5 %; *not yet* is a preserve past its date, or a missing waste log.
**Time:** 3 h.
